# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-12 (Extended v104)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Winter Year 3)**: (1) Paris—Café Musain near Panthéon (Friends of the A B C meeting); le Petit-Picpus convent district (Valjean, Cosette sanctuary); M. Gillenormand's residences; Gorbeau house (50-52, Salpêtrière district—Marius's attic cabinet); (2) English provincial harbor towns (Dunstead, Yarlby, Kelford, Staveford, Ravenmere, Ostcombe, Gulhaven, Kelmere, Dunby, Dungate, Torton). **Environmental conditions (Autumn/Winter Year 3)**: rain threatened but held off; wind off water with salt/tar smell; roads rutted and puddled after thaw; light went early; smoke lay flat; frost silvered hedges; children chased hoop; cart loaded with turnips creaked past; chalk sun on forge wall; baker's boy late; line at oven grew long.

## Primary Locations (unchanged)

**PARIS - LE PETIT-PICPUS DISTRICT**: Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus; convent complex with garden, chapel, burial vault. **M. GILLENORMAND'S RESIDENCES**: Rue Férou; Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire in Marais. **CAFÉ MUSAIN**: Near Panthéon, Rue Saint-Michel; headquarters Friends of the A B C; back room with argand lamp, two windows, private stairway on Rue des Grès. **GORBEAU HOVEL**: 50-52, Salpêtrière district; Marius's attic cabinet rented for 30 francs annually. **Other Paris locations**: Quai des Orfévres (engraver); Saint-Sulpice Chapel; Place Saint-Michel; Rue Saint-Jacques; Rousseau's restaurant opposite Basset's stamp-dealer, corner Rue des Mathurins. **VERNON**: Colonel Pontmercy's residence; grave in Vaugirard cemetery.

## Jean Valjean and Cosette (unchanged status)

Valjean integrated into convent life as assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Spiritual transformation complete—meditations on grace, humility, prayer. Cosette became convent scholar; thinks herself his daughter; adores him. Fauchelevent remains sole ally aware of full presence; grateful, talkative peasant of Picardy. Nuns do not suspect.

## Javert's Pursuit (Autumn Year 3)

Attached to Paris police after Valjean's escape. Investigated child abduction memory; followed mysterious lodger to Gorbeau house; hired room, listened at door. Valjean foiled spy by silence. Old woman warned Javert lodger intended to leave; Javert waited with two men at night. Valjean escaped via cut street lantern rope (Mouffetard); Javert followed from tree to tree but did not arrest hastily. **Current status (Autumn Year 3)**: Established sentinels, organized traps and ambuscades; sure convict could not be far off.

## Marius Pontmercy: Intellectual and Material Transformation

**Identity and family**: Son of Colonel Pontmercy (Vernon residence); mother Madame Pontmercy (née Gillenormand, died 1815). Raised by grandfather M. Gillenormand (Rue Férou, then Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire).

**Paternal legacy**: Colonel's written instruction: "The Emperor made me a Baron...my son shall take it and bear it." Also: "At Waterloo, sergeant Thénardier saved my life...If my son meets him, he will do all the good he can." **Lost document (critical)**: While Nicolette moved Marius's duds, medallion of black shagreen containing colonel's paper fell on attic staircase; never found. Marius convinced grandfather burned it; knew few lines by heart; paper was "his very heart."

**Intellectual transformation**: Converted from childhood royalism to passionate Bonapartism after reading bulletins/memoirs. Ordered hundred cards from Quai des Orfévres engraver bearing name: _Le Baron Marius Pontmercy_. Became thoroughgoing revolutionist, profoundly democratic and republican.

**Quest for Thénardier**: Went to Montfermeil to obey father's injunction; sought old sergeant; Thénardier's inn closed, no one knew what became of him. Away from house four days.

**Violent quarrel with grandfather (Autumn Year 3)**: Returned from Vernon third day, threw off travelling-coat and black ribbon. M. Gillenormand held one of Marius's cards. Marius declared father was humble heroic man who served Republic gloriously; died forgotten. Grandfather sprang to feet, cried all who served Bonaparte were brigands and cowards at Waterloo. Marius quivered like priest beholding sacred wafers cast to winds—impossible to insult grandfather yet equally impossible to leave father unavenged. Old man wheeled to bust of Duc de Berry on chimney, made profound bow, paced in silence. Marius went forth in indignation.

**Meeting Friends of the A B C (Autumn Year 3)**: Marius perceived in cabriolet at Place Saint-Michel by Laigle de Meaux; bag displayed name "MARIUS PONTMERCY." Became Courfeyrac's friend in few days. **Next day**: Courfeyrac introduced Marius to Café Musain. Whispered: "I must give you your entry to the revolution." Presented him to comrades as "A pupil."

**Evening of spiritual turmoil (Winter Year 3)**: That evening—following heated philosophical debates at Café Musain regarding grandfather's opinions versus father's legacy—left Marius profoundly shaken, melancholy shadow in his soul. Felt like earth torn open with iron for grain; felt only wound; quiver of germ and joy of fruit arrive later. Recognized life contains obscure heroes performing mysterious triumphs in petty combats, defending themselves against necessities and turpitudes; noble and mysterious, saluted with no trumpet blast.

**Intellectual distress (Autumn/Winter Year 3)**: Solitary by habit and taste, Marius now fluttered by covey of young men. Various initiatives solicited his attention; tumultuous movements of minds at liberty set his ideas in whirl. Heard unexpected talk of philosophy, literature, art, history, religion; glimpsed strange aspects but could not place them in proper perspective—suspected chaos. On abandoning grandfather's opinions for father's, supposed himself fixed; now suspected with uneasiness he was not. Angle at which he saw everything displaced anew. Odd internal upsetting; almost suffered from it.

**Material destitution (Winter Year 3)**: Swept own landing; bought sou's worth of Brie cheese at fruiterer's; waited until twilight to slip into baker's and purchase loaf, carried furtively to attic. Glided into butcher's shop awkwardly, carrying big books, timid yet angry air; removed hat from brow with perspiration drops; made profound bow to butcher's astonished wife; asked for mutton cutlet; paid six or seven sous; wrapped it in paper, put under arm between two books. On this cutlet cooked for himself, he lived for three days.

**Mourning and poverty (Winter Year 3)**: Still in mourning for father when revolution of thought occurred. Had not put off black garments, but garments quitting him. Day came when no coat remained. Trousers would go next. Courfeyrac gave him old coat; for thirty sous, Marius got it turned by porter—became new coat, but green. Marius ceased to go out until after nightfall so coat appeared black. Wished always to appear in mourning; clothed himself with night.

**Admission to law practice (Winter Year 3)**: Got admitted to practice as lawyer despite poverty. Supposed to live in Courfeyrac's room (decent, with law-books and dilapidated romance volumes serving as required library). Had letters addressed to Courfeyrac's quarters.

**Letter to grandfather (Winter Year 3)**: Informed M. Gillenormand of admission in letter cold but full of submission and respect. Grandfather trembled taking letter, read it, tore into four pieces, threw in waste-basket. Two or three days later, Mademoiselle Gillenormand heard father alone in room talking aloud to himself (always did when greatly agitated): "If you were not a fool, you would know that one cannot be a baron and a lawyer at the same time."

**Financial independence achieved (Winter Year 3)**: Passed worst straits; narrow pass opening out. By toil, perseverance, courage, will, managed to draw about seven hundred francs yearly from work. Learned German and English; thanks to Courfeyrac, put in communication with publisher friend; filled modest post of utility man in publishing house literature. Drew up prospectuses, translated newspapers, annotated editions, compiled biographies. Net product: seven hundred francs year in and year out.

**Living arrangements and budget (Winter Year 3)**: Occupied Gorbeau house cabinet (attic den minus fireplace) for 30 francs annually; contained only indispensable furniture he owned. Gave 3 francs monthly to old principal tenant for sweeping and bringing hot water every morning, fresh egg, penny roll. **Breakfast**: 2-4 sous (egg and roll). **Dinner**: 6-sou plate meat, 3-sous half vegetables, 3-sous dessert, 3 sous bread, water; 1 sou to waiter; received smile from Madam Rousseau (plump, rosy, majestic); total 16 sous. **Daily food cost**: 20 sous (365 francs yearly). **Expenses**: 30 francs rent + 36 francs old woman + trifles = 450 francs total sustenance. **Clothing**: 100 francs. **Linen and washing**: 50 + 50 = 100 francs. **Total**: 650 francs. He was rich; sometimes lent 10 francs to friend; Courfeyrac once borrowed 60 francs. **Fire**: Had no fireplace; "simplified matters."

**Wardrobe (Winter Year 3)**: Two complete black suits—one old "for every day," one brand new for special occasions. Three shirts total: one worn, one in commode, one at washerwoman's. Shirts always ragged; buttoned coat to chin. Renewed shirts as they wore out.

**Philosophy of debt and pride (Winter Year 3)**: Years required to attain flourishing condition; hard, difficult years. Had not failed single day; endured everything in destitution; done everything except contract debts. Never owed anyone sou. Debt was beginning of slavery; creditor worse than master—master possesses person, creditor possesses dignity. Rather than borrow, went without food; passed many days fasting. Feeling all extremes meet, lowered fortunes may lead to baseness of soul, kept jealous watch on pride. Such formalities or actions that in other situations seemed mere deference now seemed insipidity; nerved himself against it. Face wore severe flush. Timid even to rudeness.

## Friends of the A B C (Revolutionary Organization)

**Context (Autumn Year 3)**: Revolutionary quiver vaguely current; breaths from '89 and '93 in air. Youth moulting; people undergoing transformation through movement of age. Royalists becoming liberals; liberals turning democrats. Dark underminings throwing off shoots—the Cougourde at Aix; at Paris existed Friends of the A B C.

**Identity and purpose**: Declared themselves Friends of the A B C—the _Abaissé_,—the debased (the people). Wished to elevate people. Not numerous; secret society in embryonic state, almost coterie. Old map of France under Republic nailed to wall.

**Meetings (Autumn/Winter Year 3)**: Convened back room Café Musain; argand lamp lighted. Nearly all haranguing at haphazard; tossed words, caught up in turn; chattering in quarters. Peaceable tumults—game and uproar as much as conversation. Sarcasms, sallies, jests, French _entrain_ and English humor; merry bombardment of dialogue. Abrupt turns; perspective changes suddenly.

**Members and characteristics**: Enjolras (believer, sober), Combeferre, Jean Prouvaire, Feuilly, Courfeyrac, Bahorel, Lesgle/Laigle de Meaux, Joly, Grantaire. Most students, cordial with working classes.

**Joly**: "Malade imaginaire" junior; at twenty-three thought himself valetudinarian; placed bed head-south foot-north to avoid globe's electric current; felt pulse during thunderstorms. Otherwise gayest; young, maniacal, puny, merry; eccentric and agreeable.

**Lesgle (Laigle de Meaux)**: Ancestor keeper of hounds surnamed Lesgueules; king smiled at non-Bonaparte orthography, gave posting office of Meaux. Full of resources despite persecutions of fate. **Law school incident**: Erased from roll by professor Blondeau due to misidentification as Pontmercy. Blondeau gazed with gentleness of tiger: "If you are Pontmercy, you are not Laigle." Declared himself delighted; erasure saved him from lawyer profession.

**Grantaire**: Sceptic; scepticism as caries of intelligence. Lived with irony; axiom: "There is but one certainty, my full glass." Sneered at all devotion; said of crucifix: "gibbet which has been success." Rover, gambler, libertine, often drunk; hummed constantly "J'aimons les filles, et j'aimons le bon vin" (Vive Henri IV). Disdained Enjolras as unaccepted Pylades yet ever returning. Called him "What fine marble!"

**Courfeyrac**: Honorable fellow; wit transmitted through generations. Difference between him and predecessor Tholomyès very great—district attorney in Tholomyès, paladin in Courfeyrac.

## English Provincial Towns (Updated)

**Population movements and births**: Yera Haskick left Dunstead for Kelmere; Rinelle quit Kelford for Torton; Kadrek Brackick followed to Torton. **Births (Dunstead)**: Son Ferald Stenworth and daughter Isvie Stenworth born to Luwyn Brackick. **Claims and rumors**: Lurald Stenworth told Thizek Stenenridge deed to Kelmere pastures forged. **Rumor (Ismira)**: Wenelle Lindmere drowned crossing estuary (no body seen); granary fire was set on purpose. **Letter (burned)**: Kadan Corrley burned letter from Yera Haskick revealing Stenenridge mill ledger rewritten after flood. **Individuals and observations**: Harine Lindmere laughed at story nobody else found funny. Rinelle fell asleep in chair before fire caught; spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Pelde Stenworth looked tired, did not deny it. Kadrek Brackick meant to go to Ravenmere before frost; roads flooded, journey put off; complained of aching back. Kassa Stenson/Gadan Corrley discussed price of salt as scandal; Gadan fell asleep in chair before fire caught; watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly; argued over oats price. Rorald told everyone Islan Thornmere drowned crossing estuary (no body seen). Davus laughed at story nobody else found funny; asked "Will it rain?" Rinelle shrugged. Harine remarked "I heard river is up again" (Pelde said always was in spring).
